articles.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
articles.text:
GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. OpenAI:

We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work.

They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol. I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models.
6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions.
GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20).
Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra. The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this:

I have a full comparison grid here, but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases:

I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI:

Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

Here's Sol and here's Astra. Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon.
This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time:

I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting:

https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html  are two videos of the same thing by two different models
I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second
I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned.
Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels

Then later:

OK make it 20s

Here's the exported transcript.
The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example:

When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on.
I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?"

articles.sourceTitle: Google’s AI feature in Search gets its own incognito mode
articles.title: Google's AI feature in Search gets its own incognito mode
articles.text:
Image Credits:TechCrunch / Google

Google’s AI feature in Search gets its own incognito mode

10:04 AM PST · November 18, 2026

Google’s search engine has long offered an incognito mode for all those search queries you don’t want logged or associated with your account. Now, Google’s AI Mode in Search is getting a similar feature. In a blog post, the company announced a new feature that brings “temporary threads” to AI Mode, where the conversations you have won’t be resurfaced later in areas like your search history or recommendations.

Many leading AI chatbots already offer the option for temporary chats, Google Gemini included. However, there was not yet an option to have a temporary chat when you’re searching Google and are dropped into its conversational interface, known as AI Mode.

Image Credits:Google

Google says that users won’t have to adjust their settings to take advantage of the new option. Instead, they’ll be able to click a temporary threads icon in the upper right corner of AI Mode to engage in a temporary chat. This essentially works the same as a temporary chat would in the stand-alone Gemini chatbot.

The option could be convenient to use at those times when you start digging deeper into a particular topic via AI Mode and realize that you don’t want the discussion to become a part of your search history because of its personal nature.

Once the temporary thread is started, the session becomes detached from your account, Google says. This means that the responses the AI provides won’t be informed by past preferences, nor will they impact future personalization. That could also be useful for those times when you want to learn about something as more of a one-off, but don’t want Google to start to think of the topic as one of your main interests.

When you close out of the thread, you will return to searching as usual.

The company says the option to engage in temporary chats in AI Mode is rolling out globally on desktop and mobile across all supported languages.

Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie, an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them.So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds.Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser.Experience Genie 4 in Project GenieWith Genie 4, our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue.

Discover new Genie 3 capabilitiesWhile Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include:Extended sessions and world chaining: Explore for up to 3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds), or link multiple worlds together for longer journeys.360-degree panorama image grounding: Seed new worlds from 360-degree panorama images.Real-time in-world events: Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore.

Create new interactive experiencesThe new Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood.You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds.

Explore the new galleryWhen you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.”

The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism.Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix.Learn how we are building responsiblyWe are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings.Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. articles.sourceTitle: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
articles.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
articles.text:
Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage.
For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work.

A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review."

News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat
Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff
Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found.
In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it.

What the Harvard data measured
How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data.
The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months.
The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI.
The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report.
Drafts went up and finished issues did not
With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start.
Output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira issues resolved, and an issue counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written.
The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat issue count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of issues by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review.
Where the shortfall shows up: the review queue
The paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code showed no measurable change.
AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer said, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity.
That account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology. Anyone buying an agent should care which channel dominates, because the two call for different spending.
Employment did not move either
Nor did the coding gains show up as job cuts. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent. A noisier estimate rules out a decline in engineering employment larger than 13.8 percent. The authors caution that these are short-run effects measured in partial equilibrium, which could mask job losses at competing firms, and that the assistant estimate for engineering employment shows upward pre-trends that make it hard to read causally.
Legal AI tools are designed around a similar checkpoint
Those software results arrive as legal AI tools adopt a related design, and the Harvey and Cooley announcements both follow it: automate a first pass, then keep a lawyer at the checkpoint. Harvey’s workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and announced Oct. 7, is the drafting case. Harvey says the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss “commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work” and that its tool produces the research and a first draft “in a matter of hours.” The announcement describes “human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer’s judgment matters most,” but it does not state how long lawyers spend at those checkpoints or how long it takes to reach a motion ready to file.
Cooley’s Oct. 8 announcement applies the same posture to a different task, since its agent recommends redactions rather than drafting arguments. Cooley says the agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court, which puts the human checkpoint at the last step before submission. As ComplexDiscovery reported Oct. 10, the announcement carries no error rate.
For a motion filed in federal court, the checkpoint is a legal duty rather than a design choice. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b), an attorney presenting a motion certifies several things about it to the best of the attorney’s knowledge, information and belief, “formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.” Its legal contentions must be “warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law.” Its factual contentions must have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, be likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. A first draft can arrive in hours, but that inquiry stays with the attorney, and the software evidence raises the possibility that review could absorb some of the drafting savings.
The paper’s method carries a second lesson, this one for information governance teams. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms’ own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as “Co-authored-by” lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. AI authorship can leave its own metadata trail in collaboration systems. That trail is a record that a retention schedule and a legal hold may need to reach.
None of this means legal work will behave like software, and the limits of the comparison matter. Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the company. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms.
Document review offers a partial precedent
Discovery practitioners have argued a version of this question before, and Austin’s post draws that comparison. He wrot

articles.sourceTitle: AI is killing All About Berlin
articles.title: AI is killing All About Berlin
articles.text:
AI is killing All About Berlin
Posted on May 26, 2026

Psst! There is an update to this post.

This is the traffic to All About Berlin, the website that I run since 2017, and live from since 2020. After 7 years of growth, it has lost 70% 75% of its traffic to Google AI Overviews.
When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic.
What it means to be first on Google
It’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience. Soon, I will need another way to pay my rent. Instead of writing new guides, I already spend my days preparing for that future.
It’s not just about the money. I have poured 8 years of my life into making something good and useful. Strangers’ faces light up when they learn that I run All About Berlin. Local and federal government offices refer people to my guides. The Berlin immigration office uses my data about themselves. It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities.
If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went.
This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer update them. It’s just not worth it.
It will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them.1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads.
I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future.

This was also discussed on Mastodon, Hacker News, LinkedIn and Twitter. If you are affected, reach out. Let me know how you are doing. You are not going through this alone.
